title: Assign responsibility for information security
officialText: Each organization shall designate an Information Security Officer to administer the organization's information security program and shall ensure management supports and is accountable for the security of state information resources.
plainEnglish: Name someone responsible for security (an Information Security Officer) and make sure leadership backs the security program. If you do business with a Texas state agency, you are expected to mirror these roles.
assessmentObjectives: [a] an Information Security Officer or equivalent role is designated in writing;
[b] responsibilities for the security program are documented; and
[c] management accountability for security is established.
whyItMatters: TAC 202 is built on clear ownership. State agencies and the vendors serving them are expected to show a named security owner before anything else.
evidenceExamples: Appointment memo or org chart naming the Information Security Officer
A security program charter signed by management
Role description listing the security owner's duties
aiReviewGuidance: Confirm a specific named role with documented responsibilities and evidence of management backing. A vague 'IT handles it' with no named owner is insufficient.
commonFailures: No one formally accountable for security
Responsibilities assumed but never written down
No management sign-off on the security program

title: Perform and document a risk assessment
officialText: Each organization shall perform risk assessments of information resources and document the risks, and shall review and update the assessment on a defined periodic basis or when significant changes occur.
plainEnglish: Regularly look at what could go wrong with your systems and data, write down those risks, and update the list when things change.
assessmentObjectives: [a] a risk assessment covering information resources has been performed;
[b] identified risks are documented with their impact; and
whyItMatters: The entire TAC 202 control baseline is applied based on risk. Without a documented assessment, control decisions cannot be justified.
evidenceExamples: A completed risk assessment report or register
A risk register spreadsheet listing threats, likelihood, and impact
Policy stating how often risk assessments are refreshed
aiReviewGuidance: Look for an actual assessment output (register or report) with a defined review cadence, not just a policy promising to do one someday.
commonFailures: Policy says 'we assess risk' but no assessment exists
Risks listed with no impact or ownership

title: Adopt a security control standards catalog and policies
officialText: Each organization shall implement a set of security controls based on the state security control standards catalog, document information security policies, and ensure controls are commensurate with the risk and magnitude of harm.
plainEnglish: Adopt written security policies based on the Texas DIR control catalog, and put controls in place that match your level of risk.
assessmentObjectives: [a] information security policies are documented and approved;
[b] controls are selected from the state control standards catalog; and
[c] controls are matched to assessed risk.
whyItMatters: The control catalog is the measuring stick DIR and state agencies use. Documented policies tied to it are what an audit checks first.
evidenceExamples: A control mapping showing which catalog controls you have implemented
Approval record showing policies were adopted by management
aiReviewGuidance: Confirm documented, approved policies plus a mapping to the state control catalog. Many CMMC controls will overlap; note where existing CMMC evidence supports a catalog control.
commonFailures: No written security policies at all
Policies copied from a template with no mapping to the DIR catalog
Controls claimed but not tied to any standard

title: Control access to state information resources
officialText: Each organization shall manage access to information resources using the principle of least privilege, authenticate users, and review access rights on a periodic basis.
plainEnglish: Give people only the access they need, make them log in securely, and review who has access regularly.
assessmentObjectives: [a] access is granted on a least-privilege basis;
[b] users are authenticated before access; and
whyItMatters: Access control is the most frequently cited weakness in state audits and overlaps directly with your CMMC Access Control work.
evidenceExamples: Access control policy describing least privilege and review cadence
Screenshot of role-based access settings or an access review log
Reference to CMMC Access Control practices you have already completed
aiReviewGuidance: Look for least-privilege assignment, authentication, and evidence of periodic access reviews. Existing CMMC AC/IA evidence frequently satisfies this; note the overlap.
commonFailures: No periodic review, so stale accounts linger
Shared logins with no individual authentication

title: Report security incidents to DIR
officialText: Each organization shall establish an incident response capability and report security incidents to the Department of Information Resources in accordance with required timeframes, including incidents that propagate to other state systems or involve significant harm.
plainEnglish: Have a plan to respond to security incidents and report qualifying incidents to the Texas Department of Information Resources (DIR) within the required time.
assessmentObjectives: [b] criteria and timeframes for reporting incidents to DIR are defined; and
[c] a reporting channel to DIR is identified.
whyItMatters: DIR incident reporting is a distinct state obligation. Knowing what and when to report keeps a local incident from becoming a statewide one.
evidenceExamples: Incident response plan that includes DIR reporting criteria and timeframes
Screenshot or link to the DIR incident-reporting portal
A reporting decision tree for when an incident must go to DIR
aiReviewGuidance: Confirm an incident response plan that explicitly covers DIR reporting criteria, timeframes, and the channel. A generic IR plan with no DIR reporting step is incomplete for this framework.
commonFailures: IR plan never mentions reporting to DIR
No defined criteria for which incidents are reportable
No one knows how to actually reach DIR

legalRef: 1 Tex. Admin. Code §202.26 / Tex. Gov't Code §2054
title: Meet security requirements for doing business with the state
officialText: A contractor or vendor providing information resources services to a state agency shall comply with applicable state information security requirements, including the controls, reporting, and assessment obligations flowed down through the agency's contract and the DIR standards.
plainEnglish: If you sell IT services or handle data for a Texas state agency, your contract flows these security rules down to you, and you must meet them.
assessmentObjectives: [a] contractual information-security obligations from state agencies are identified;
[b] the organization can demonstrate compliance with flowed-down controls; and
[c] assessment or attestation requirements in the contract are met.
whyItMatters: This is the on-ramp for selling to the State of Texas. Vendors that cannot show TAC 202 alignment lose or fail state contracts.
evidenceExamples: The security clauses from a state agency contract or RFP
A compliance matrix mapping contract requirements to your controls
Any attestation or assessment artifact provided to a state agency
aiReviewGuidance: Look for identified contractual obligations and a mapping showing how the organization meets each. If the organization does not contract with the state, this requirement may not apply and should be noted as such.
commonFailures: Signing a state contract without reading its security flow-downs
No mapping of contract requirements to actual controls
Missing a required attestation or assessment deadline
